beats.intro_line: Hi, I'm Varun, and this video is about the trap in the data — leakage, and how it fooled us.

beats.narration_text: Our data was hiding a trap. The label came from the very test we were feeding the model — so part of what looked like reasoning was leakage.

props.text:
Our data was hiding a shortcut.

beats.series_slot: BODY ¶1 — structure vs function, and the subtle part
beats.narration_text: Glaucoma is confirmed with two kinds of tests: structural ones like the O-C-T scan, and functional ones like the visual-field exam. Here's the subtle part we uncovered: in our dataset, the ground-truth label — glaucoma or not — was itself derived from the visual-field test. Structure is what the tissue looks like. Function is what the patient can actually see. They are related, but they are not the same measurement.

props.sparkLine: The label came from the test.
props.caption: The ground-truth label is derived from the visual field. Conceptual.

beats.series_slot: BODY ¶2 — THE TAUGHT CONCEPT: data leakage
beats.narration_text: So we ran the experiment that mattered. We trained a simple model on the visual-field data alone — and it scored almost perfectly. Not because it understood glaucoma. Because we'd handed it the very measurement the label was computed from. It was reading the answer key. In machine learning, this is called data leakage — when information about the answer sneaks into the input, and your dazzling score means nothing.

props.sparkLine: It was reading the answer key.
props.caption: Conceptual. No performance figure is claimed in this episode.

beats.series_slot: BODY ¶3 — what it reframed, and the honest re-run
beats.narration_text: That reframed everything. Our reasoning agents had been given the visual field — so part of their impressive performance wasn't clever deliberation at all. It was leakage. To test the honest question — can a machine reason about glaucoma from structure alone — we stripped the visual field away and re-ran the agents on the O-C-T scan only. Their performance dropped toward chance.

props.sparkLine: What the striking result was not.
lines: Partly the answer key, handed over in the input
Stripped of the visual field, performance fell toward chance
The honest problem — structure alone — was still standing
props.caption: Conceptual. Described in words; no figure is claimed.

beats.series_slot: BODY ¶4 — hard to sit with, and why it matters
beats.narration_text: That's a hard result to sit with. But it's the truth, and finding it is what makes the rest of the work trustworthy. The genuinely hard problem — predicting the diagnosis from the nerve's structure, independent of the signal that defined the label — was still standing, unsolved and honest. So we rebuilt around it.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this: when an A-I scores ninety-nine percent, the first question isn't how did it do that — it's what did I accidentally give it? Ask for the checks that catch leakage before publication, and for one real case where a celebrated medical-A-I result turned out to be reading a shortcut. If it can't name a mechanism, push back.
